$comment: Roles, not colours. A component asks for surface.raised or text.muted; it never asks
for neutral-200. That indirection is what lets dark mode and print exist at all, and
it is why a component file contains no hex values anywhere.
Each entry names a ramp step, resolved at build time. 'brand.600' means step 600 of
the generated brand ramp.
control is the one border with a contrast requirement: an empty text input is
identified by its outline and nothing else, so WCAG 1.4.11 applies to it. subtle
and default are decorative - a table rule, a card edge - and are exempt because
removing them would lose no information.
solid is step 700, not 600. At the placeholder teal's hue, step 600 sits in a
lightness dead zone where neither white (3.80:1) nor near-black (4.30:1) reaches
4.5:1 - so the primary button had no readable foreground at all. Step 700 gives
5.52:1 with white.
The dead zone moves with the hue. The contract below re-checks it, so swapping the
brand fails the test suite with a message naming this line rather than shipping an
unreadable button.
Not an inversion. Dark surfaces are a raised near-black rather than pure black:
pure black beside a bright value maximises halation, which is precisely the
smearing that makes small numerals hard to read - and small numerals are what this
system exists to display.
Text tops out at neutral.100 rather than white for the same reason.
The pairs that must meet a contrast threshold, and the pairs that are deliberately
exempt with a reason. The test suite iterates this list; it does not invent its own.
Writing it down this way is the point. An accessibility check that only tests the
pairs which happen to pass is worthless, and one that demands 3:1 of every border -
including a table rule whose removal would lose no information - fails honestly but
uselessly, and gets weakened until it passes. Every exemption here states what would
be lost if the element vanished, which is the actual WCAG test for whether it
carries meaning.

required.why: Clinical values render in text.primary. A misread digit changes a decision, so this is held to 7:1, above the AA floor.
Body text on an inset panel.
Muted is the most-abused role in any design system - it ends up on timestamps and units that people do need to read.
A link nobody can read is not a link.
The primary button label. Computed automatically, and verified here so a brand change cannot break it silently.
The label does not change on hover; the background does.
Text inside a tinted brand panel.
An empty text input is identified by its outline and nothing else. WCAG 1.4.11 applies squarely.
The same input, inside a card.
The focus ring is the only thing telling a keyboard user where they are.
WCAG exempts disabled controls, and a disabled label still has to be readable enough to know what the control would do. 3:1 keeps it legible while still reading as inactive.

statusRequired.why: The status label inside its tinted chip.
The icon is the non-colour carrier of meaning; if it cannot be seen, criterion 4 is not met.
A filled status badge. Foreground computed per status, since amber and red need opposite answers.
Status text used inline on the page rather than inside a chip.

exempt.why: A table rule or list divider. Remove it and no information is lost - the rows are still separated by spacing. WCAG 1.4.11 covers components and state, not decoration.
A card edge. The card is already delineated by its background and elevation; the border is refinement. Anything that needs a visible boundary uses border.control.

A status chip's outline. The chip is identified by its icon and its label, both of which are contrast-verified above. The outline is refinement, and forcing it to 3:1 would make every chip read as an alert.

exempt.pair: state.hoverOverlay, state.selected, state.skeleton on any surface
exempt.why: Transient or placeholder surfaces that carry no information on their own. A skeleton that met 3:1 against the page would look like content.
The boundary of a control that cannot be operated. Its state is already carried by the disabled text colour and by aria-disabled.

$comment: The heart of the palette, and the part with a safety property attached.
Every status carries an icon and a bilingual label alongside its colour, and the
type system requires all three. That is what makes acceptance criterion 4 -
'colour is never the sole carrier of meaning' - structural rather than a rule
someone has to remember: a status with no icon does not typecheck, and the test
suite asserts that any two statuses which collapse together under colour-blindness
simulation have different icons.
priority orders them when several apply to one value; higher wins.
Bengali labels need Dr. Nahid's review - they are clinical terms, and this is his
professional register, not a translator's. Recorded against D-24 (terminology).

$comment: Which ramp step each status role uses, per theme. One mapping for all seven
statuses: a status that needed its own steps would be one whose contrast nobody
had checked.
solid is 700 for the same reason brand.solid is: at step 600 every one of the
seven statuses landed between 4.05:1 and 4.36:1 with its best foreground - all
just under AA, none of them obviously wrong to the eye. That is precisely the
band where a design system ships an accessibility failure it cannot see.
